Starting next class, we will use __normalized scientific notation__ to represent both very large and very small numbers. In this notation, any number can be represented by a number (called the "coefficient") greater than $$1.0$$ and less than $$10,$$ multiplied by ten to some power. For example, here are some numbers written in both the ordinary decimal notation and in normalized scientific notation.

The word "normalized" in "normalized scientific notation" means that the coefficient is greater than or equal to $$1$$ and less than $$10.$$ For example, $$42.1 \times 10^5$$ is in scientific notation, but not normalized scientific notation. In normalized scientific notation, we'd write $$4.21 \times 10^6$$ instead. Throughout this class, you should default to using normalized scientific notation.

$$\begin{tabular}{ r | r } \text{decimal notation} & \text{normalized scientific notation} \\ \hline 350 & $$3.50 \times 10^2\,\,\;$$ \\ 10{,}005 & $$1.0005 \times 10^4\,\,\;$$ \\ 14.3 & $$1.43 \times 10^1\,\,\;$$ \\ 578{,}240.92 & $$5.7824092 \times 10^5\,\,\;$$\\ 0.00037 & $$3.7 \times 10^{-4}$$ \end{tabular}$$

If you haven't learned about scientific notation before or would like some extra practice, please go to the "Prep Work" tab and work through the "Scientific Notation" reading. (If you already are comfortable with scientific notation, you can skip this.)

This question is a short practice problem to make sure you are ready to use scientific notation in upcoming classes.

Suppose a student wants to find the moment of mass $$Mx$$ for some lever and measures $$\begin{aligned} M & = 7 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{g} \\ x & = 3 \times 10^2 \;\mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}$$

What is the moment of mass in normalized scientific notation?

statement:
Part A. In class, we built an equation to help us understand how levers work. In this problem (which has several parts), we'll do the same to help us understand how ramps work.

Below is an image of the sort of ramp we're talking about. It's used to make it easier to lift heavy loads, in this case into a truck.

__image credit: https://handiramp.com/product/aluminum-walk-ramp-type-a-38in-wide-16ft-long/__

Let's begin with some exploratory research.

Build your own ramp using whatever materials you have around. One easy way to do this is to use a hardcover book (you can simply tilt the cover to different angles to make ramps of different heights). We also found that a tablet with a kickstand and a felt cover worked well (it was easy to adjust how steep the ramp is.) A piece of corrugated cardboard would also make a good ramp. Feel free to use whatever you have around. Below is a picture of our ramp: Once you have a ramp, take a small toy car which rolls freely (i.e. a car on which you can spin the wheels easily) and push it up your ramp. (If you don't have a small toy car, you can try something else that rolls. We used a small cylindrical tube.) Push the car up the ramp with one finger. Take note of how much force you need to use to push the car up the ramp (you should be able to feel this with your finger).

Based on your exploratory research, does it take more force to push something up

a steep ramp

a shallow ramp

It's the total height of the ramp, not how steep or shallow it is, determines how much force you feel with your finger

It's the same force for all ramps.

Part B. Now that we have done some exploratory research, it's time to define a specific problem we want to solve with our quantitative model.

For the law of the lever, we asked when a lever would be balanced. Let's ask a similar question for a ramp.

We have a ramp with a box on it. We will call that box $$A.$$ Then we tie a rope to that box. The rope goes over a pulley at the end of the ramp and then is attached to a second box, box $$B,$$ which hangs from the rope. This setup is shown below.

Throughout our analysis, we will ignore the mass of the rope (it's very thin and light) and assume there is no friction.

Based on your exploratory research, which of the following is the best description of when such a ramp will be balanced?

When box $$B$$ has the same mass as box $$A.$$

When box $$B$$ is less massive than box $$A.$$

When box $$B$$ is more massive than box $$A.$$

In class, our first step in creating an equation for a lever was to decide which features of a lever to keep in our equation and which to ignore. Let's use about the same level of detail for the ramp as we did when writing an equation for levers in class.

If you're familiar with the idea of friction, don't include it. In class, we ignored friction in the seesaw. To make a simple model, we leave friction out. More detailed models could account for it, be we will not do that here.

Which **two** of the following features would we **not** account for in our equation for the force needed to push an object up a ramp? Select all that apply.

the slope of the ramp

the material the ramp is made from

the mass of the ramp

the mass of box $$A$$

the mass of box $$B$$

Next, we would like some different hypotheses to test. Remember that when we studied the law of the lever, we built an equation template for balancing, $$\text{stuff on left side of lever} = \text{stuff on right side of lever}$$

We would like to do something similar for the ramp, since the boxes are balancing each other on the ramp: $$\text{stuff on ramp} = \text{stuff hanging}.$$

This time, $$\text{``stuff''}$$ needs to consist of the masses of the boxes and the slope of the ramp and nothing else, since that's all we've included in our mathematization.

The slope is a ratio of side lengths of the ramp, so in order to understand a little better where this hypothesis comes from, let's redraw our diagram and include side lengths of the ramp measurements. Part H. We've already chosen a single best quantitative hypothesis for when a ramp is balanced. We'd like to go back and understand what this hypothesis means a little better. To do that, we'll turn the equation for the hypothesis into an equation using the side lengths of the ramp.

**Which one of the following is equivalent to our best quantitative hypothesis? **

$$\text{hypotenuse}$$ means the length of the hypotenuse of the ramp. $$\text{height}$$ means the height of the ramp, and $$\text{width}$$ means the length of the horizontal segment at the bottom of the ramp, called $$x$$ in the previous part of the problem.

In the final lesson of the class, we will return to this interpretation of our ramp hypothesis and try to understand it in the same framework as the law of the lever.

$$M_A \cdot \text{hypotenuse} = M_B \cdot \text{height}$$

$$\dfrac{M_A}{\text{height}} = \dfrac{M_B}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$

$$\dfrac{M_A}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{M_B}{\text{height}}$$

Part I. Most archaeologists believe that the ancient Egyptians used very long ramps while building the pyramids. (It's also likely that ancient Egyptians used levers and ramps in combination.) The ramps had to be long because long ramps are shallow, and the stones the Egyptians assembled into the pyramids were too heavy to lift up steep ramps.

The stones in the upper layers of Khufu's pyramid have a mass of about $$2 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ $$(2000 \;\mathrm{kg})$$ each.

The pyramids were primarily built by farmers, laboring in the seasons when there was no farm work to do. Let's estimate that a single worker can exert a force big enough to pick a $$60 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ stone straight up. (This means $$60 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ can play the role of "mass B" from our analysis of a ramp.)

What is the steepest slope for the ramp the ancient Egyptians could have used if each block was to be pushed (and pulled with ropes) by a team of 8 workers?

You can neglect friction for this problem. Although there was friction between the ramp and stone blocks during construction of the pyramids, ancient Egyptians put the stones on sleds, likely lubricated with water, to reduce the friction as much as possible.

This is an estimation problem, so your answer only needs to be approximately correct.

In physics, "estimate" does not mean "take a guess at the answer right away". Instead, it means that you can round things off or make approximations as you work through a problem. You should still use the principles of physics, especially the quantitative hypothesis for how ramps work developed in the earlier parts of this question, as you make your estimate. In fact, much of the estimating has been done for you here, since the problem estimates the mass of a farm worker. In future weeks, you might have to estimate that mass yourself as one part of estimating the slope of the ramps.

statement:
**About writing problems**

In weeks 1, 4, 7, and 10, our homework has one __writing problem__. This is a problem to which you submit your work to AoPS and our graders give you personalized feedback. This week, you will conduct a qualitative experiment on a new type of lever and report your results.

Your goal is to practice making observations and writing them down clearly so that other scientists can understand your work. You will also practice making and testing hypotheses. You can hand-write your lab report on lined notebook paper, graph paper, or blank paper. You are also welcome to type your response. Be sure to keep your work neat and label each part. You are welcome to draw pictures to explain your work.

A style note: In AoPS math courses, students are often encouraged to use "we" in writing problem solutions. E.g. "We will factor this quadratic equation" rather than "I will factor this quadratic equation." That is a norm in mathematics, but not a universal norm in physics. Professional physics style guides allow using either "I" or "we" when writing a scientific report, so feel free to use whichever feels more natural to you when working on writing problems.

**This week's problem**

Below are pictures of a lever with the fulcrum at the end instead of in the middle. The load (the little pot in the pictures) is between the applied force (from the hand) and the fulcrum. This setup is called a __class 2 lever__.

With this type of lever, you can place a load at three different positions, as shown. Then you can lift the lever. Sometimes, it will take more force to lift the lever and sometimes less, depending on which position the load is in.

Make a hypothesis about when it will require more force and when it will require less to lift the lever. Then build a lever and try it out. You do not need to use the same supplies as those shown in the picture; you can build your lever using any supplies you have available.

Write a report on your experiment. The goal of the report is to explain what you did in this experiment, why you did it, and what you found. A report like this is called a __lab report__.

You do not need to use special formatting or sections in your lab report, but it should be clear enough that someone who wasn't part of our class and didn't previously know about levers could still understand it.

Make sure you include: - What you were trying to figure out by doing an experiment. - What your hypothesis was and why you had that hypothesis. - What your result was, and how it related to your hypothesis.

Your report doesn't need to be long. One page is likely enough.

Although we did a quantitative analysis of the law of the lever in class, this experiment is intended to be qualitative. You don't need to include equations in your report.

In most lab reports, you would also include an explanation of how you built your lever, what supplies you used, etc. However, you may omit that this week. This will keep your report from becoming too long.

**note:** In this class, all your submissions to writing problem should stand completely on their own. For example, you shouldn't reference "position 1", "position 2", and "position 3", meaning the positions from the photo in this problem, without explaining what those positions are. Although your grader will understand what you mean because they have access to the problem, they will grade as if they do not understand what you mean. It's your job to explain your thoughts from scratch. We are practicing writing material that can be understood without referencing the problem itself because this is an important skill in communication in science. You can, however, assume that the grader has a basic scientific understanding, can follow algebra steps, knows what technical terms taught in this course mean, etc.

statement:
The goal of this problem is to show you some common measurement devices and get you thinking about how they work. To do that, it introduces a new distinction: the distinction between digital and analog devices.

-----------------------------------------

Measurement devices are either __digital__ or __analog__. A digital device is one that reads out one of a "discrete" means "not smooth" or "discontinuous" set of readings.

An analog device is one that can move smoothly between values. For example, below are pictured an analog thermometer and a digital thermometer. __Analog thermometer. By Doggo19292 - Own work, Attribution, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=102933605__

This is an analog thermometer because the red liquid in the tube can move smoothly to higher or lower values. There are discrete lines on the side of the thermometer, but those are to assist with the reading. The measurement is made by the height of the red column, which advances smoothly.

__Digital thermometer. Popka, product image from Amazon__

This is a digital thermometer because the only readout is one that advances in discrete jumps. In this case, those jumps are $$0.1^\circ \mathrm{C}.$$

Below are images of measuring instruments, along with brief descriptions of what they measure. Categorize each according to whether it is digital or analog.

**a)** This is a multimeter. It is used in electric circuits to measure the voltage, current, or resistance between different parts of the circuit. It reads out voltage, for example, to the nearest thousandth of a volt on its display. __By Binarysequence - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=23376138__

**b)** A tape measure used to measure lengths of a few meters. __By User Moriori on en.wikipedia - Photo taken by User:Moriori for Ruler article, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=989462__

**c)** These calipers are used to measure distances to higher accuracy than a ruler. The length is read off from the electronic display, which advances in units of $$0.01 \;\mathrm{mm}.$$ __By Jacek Halicki - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=86354986__

**d)** A simple bathroom scale. When the user stands on it, the dial with numbers spins to show the weight. __Sears, https://www.sears.com/taylor-scales-analog-bath-scale-white/p-08311839000P__

**e)** This home radio has a knob you can turn to change the station. As you smoothly turn the knob, the frequency that the radio is tuned to changes. __Tolga Sipahi, Getty Images__

Part A. In this two-part problem, you'll practice figuring out how to find conversion factors given some information about units presented in paragraph form. The challenge is to read the information, understand how it can be used to create conversion factors, and then use those conversion factors to answer the question. Part (A) is shorter and you may or may not need a conversion factor for it. In part (B), there will be more conversions to make.

-------------------------------

From 1793 - 1805, France used the "French Republican Calendar" to keep track of time. Under this system, each day was divided into ten hours, each hour was divided into 100 minutes, and each minute into 100 seconds. Because these lengths of time are not the same as ordinary hours, minutes, and seconds, we can call them "FR hours", "FR minutes", and "FR seconds", short for "French Republican hours", etc. So a day was equal to ten FR hours, an FR hour was equal to 100 FR minutes, etc. The length of one day was the same in this system as in the current, modern one.

France no longer uses this calendar. Instead, they use the same definition of hours, minutes, and seconds that people in the US and all other countries around the world do, with 24 hours in a day, 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 seconds in a minute. In this problem we'll imagine France was going to convert back to the French Republican Calendar and figure out the consequences.

Aside from a few highways and roads in cities, most French roads today use the same speed limit, which is currently $$80 \dfrac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{hour}}.$$ (France uses kilometers, not miles to measure distance. This speed limit is approximately 50 mph. France lowered the speed limit to this value in 2018 in a successful attempt to reduce traffic accident deaths. The speed limit is also lower than this when conditions are wet or otherwise dangerous.)

If France were to convert to using FR hours again, how would we write the speed limit in France, assuming drivers should go no faster or slower than before the unit change?

The definition of the kilometer does not change in this scenario.

statement:
The lesson for this problem is that you don't necessarily need to know where a mathematical expression comes from or what it's an expression for in order to make some sense of it. Here, we'll use dimensions to figure out what type of thing (a length, an area, or a volume) various expressions represent. All the expressions in this problem are real mathematical expressions that you could come across in science or math problems, but you don't need to know what problems they come from in order to figure out what type of thing these expressions represent!

------------------------------------

Each of the following expressions is in terms of some variables. All the variables represent a length of some kind. For example, the variable $$\color{red}{a}\color{black}$$ might be the side length of a rectangle and the variable $$\color{red}{r}\color{black}$$ might be the radius of a circle. In this problem, the exact interpretation of each variable is not important. What matters is that each variable is some length. ($$\pi$$ is not a variable. It is a number with no dimensions. The variables are $$\color{red}{a}\color{black}, \color{red}{b}\color{black}, \color{red}{c}\color{black}, \color{red}{d}\color{black}, \color{red}{\ell}\color{black}, \color{red}{h}\color{black}, \color{red}{r}\color{black}, \color{red}{r_1}\color{black}, \color{red}{r_2}\color{black}$$ and $$\color{red}{R}\color{black}.$$ We've colored them red to help you recognize which symbols are variables.)

Classify each expression according to whether it is for a length, an area, or a volume.

The __Dictyostelium discoideum__ is an amoeba, a single-celled organism. Under ordinary circumstances, when viewed under a microscope, the amoebas will look like separate individual cells:

__Dictyostelium discoideum__, however, is a __slime mold__. As part of their lifecycle, the individual amoeba aggregate, forming a film, and then grow into a slug shape. (There are several other shapes that the aggregations take at various stages of the life cycle. Below are several slugs as well as a few other shapes.)

Scientists wanted to know how many individual amoeba cells go into a slug. To figure this out, they estimated the volume of an individual amoeba and the volume of a slug, then did arithmetic to find the number of amoeba in a slug.

In 1953, two scientists, Bonner and Frascella, estimated the diameter of a single __Dictyostelium discoideum__ to be $$8 \;\mathrm{\mu m}.$$ (Remember that $$1 \;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ is one __micrometer__, or $$10^{-6} \;\mathrm{m}.)$$ They also measured the volume of a __Dictyostelium discoideum__ slug. With these measurements, they estimated there are about $$100{,}000$$ amoeba in a single slug.

In 1998, Bonner returned to the problem and used new methods to estimate the diameter of a single amoeba. This time, he found $$4 \;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ for the average diameter. Bonner did not change his estimate of the volume of a slug between 1953 and 1998. He also didn't change his assumptions about the shape of amoeba, just the overall scale.

Bonner used his updated diameter measurement to re-estimate the number of amoeba in a single slug. What was his new estimate?

(You should enter a number as your answer. To answer this problem, try thinking about the dimensions of the quantities involved; you won't need to use any geometric volume formulas.)

-------------------

Converting between temperature scales is a little different than most unit conversions, such as those for length. This is because for temperature scales, the zero can mean different things in different scales. For example, $$0^\circ\mathrm{F} = -\dfrac{160}{9}^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

There are two common temperature scales that do have the same zero, called __absolute zero__. These are the Kelvin and Rankine scales.

A temperature of $$0^\circ \mathrm{C}$$ corresponds to a temperature $$273.15 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ The Kelvin and Celsius scales are set up so that increasing any temperature by $$1 \;\mathrm{K}$$ also increases that temperature by $$1^\circ \mathrm{C}.$$

Like the Kelvin and Celsius scales, the Fahrenheit and Rankine scales use the same step size between degrees, but have a constant offset from each other. A temperature change of $$1^\circ \mathrm{C}$$ is the same as a temperature increase of $$\dfrac95^\circ$$ in Fahrenheit or Rankine.

The Fahrenheit and Celsius scales have the same numerical value at $$-40^\circ,$$ meaning $$-40^\circ \mathrm{F} = -40^\circ \mathrm{C}.$$

At what numerical value do the Kelvin and Fahrenheit scales have the same temperature?

Do not include units in your answer for this question, since it's asking about two different units simultaneously. Just give the numerical part of the answer. Do not round your answer; the data given above about the temperature scales is exact, so your answer here should be exact and include all the decimal places.

The goal of the problem is to show you how, even if you don't understand everything about a physical scenario or everything about where a formula comes from, you can still often make progress just by thinking about dimensions.

Using a technique called the __Doppler shift__, astronomers are able to measure how fast distant stars are moving towards or away from Earth.

In 1995, astronomers measuring star Pegasi 51 noticed that the star was coming towards Earth, then moving away, then coming towards Earth again in a regular manner. Their data looked like this:

__image credit: Pearson Education__

Astronomers realized that the reason the star seemed to be shaking back and forth in the sky was that it had a planet orbiting it. Although they couldn't see the planet directly, they knew that the planet's gravity was alternately tugging the star towards and away from Earth, depending on where the planet was in its orbit. It was by examining this graph that astronomers discovered the first known planets around other stars.

Astronomers wanted to know more about the planet orbiting Pegasi 51. One thing they did was draw a horizontal bar beneath all the data points in the plot to indicate the __period__ $$P$$ of the orbit. This is the time it takes the planet to make one complete trip around Pegasi 51. Astronomers also knew that finding the period would help them figure out how far away the planet was from the star, which would help them figure out how hot the planet might be and whether it might support life.

According to the theory of Newtonian mechanics, the distance $$a$$ between a star and a planet is $$a = \left( G (m_1+m_2) \left(\dfrac{P}{2\pi}\right)^2 \right)^n$$ for some number $$n.$$

In this equation, $$G$$ is the gravitational constant from Newton's formula in the previous part of this problem. $$m_1$$ is the mass of the planet and $$m_2$$ is the mass of the star.

$$n$$ has no dimensions; it is just a number. What is the exact value of $$n?$$ (Do not use a decimal approximation for this problem.)

statement:
One of the most important parts of learning is asking questions. Questions are an important mode of communication between students and instructors, and from student to student.

You can ask questions during class, on the message boards, and when chatting with other students in the classroom outside class hours. When you ask them a question, everyone benefits: other students may have had the same question, and instructors learn more about what students are working on.

Below is the AoPS advice on how to ask a good question:

Most often, we ask others questions to get answers. But at AoPS, we won't just tell you what the next step is or what you need to do in order to get a perfect score. Instead, we'll help you understand the material and ask questions that help you develop your own critical thinking skills. This will allow you to solve the problem on your own.

Some students may find this frustrating because the homework is due that day, and they just want to be told what to do. Please understand that you will not learn as much this way, and we will not just give you the answer or solution.

**Moderate Level Question-Asking: Be Specific**

Statements like "Please help" or "I'm stuck" are very hard to answer. After all, there aren't any details there! These statements will generally get a response of "What do you need help with?" or "What are you stuck on?" or "What don't you understand?"

In order to get help, think carefully about what you're are stuck on and try to tell us about it in your question. Some examples are: "I don't understand what the question means when it says ____." "Can someone explain how (some property) applies to this problem?"

**Expert Level Question-Asking: Providing Background**

In addition to asking specific questions, great questions include some background. If we know about what you have already tried or how you're thinking about the problem, it will help us give better, more relevant tips. Expert-level questions look like this:

"I tried (some approach), but now I'm stuck. Can someone give me a hint?" "It seems like we can use (some property) on this problem. I can tell how it applies ____ but I'm stuck on how it works with ____. Any tips?"

Knowing what you are having trouble with is an important skill to develop. To help us assist you in the best way, try to figure out specifically what is stopping you from moving forward. Try to make your question as specific as possible. We are here to help you, but we need some information to directly respond to your inquiry.

**Getting Started**

Regarding homework questions, AoPS has a general policy that students should get the discussion started. If you tell us you have no idea how to start, we will prompt you to come up with an idea to get the ball rolling. It doesn't even have to be a good idea, but looking at a problem and coming up with ideas is an important problem-solving skill that we want you to practice. After you get in the habit of coming up with ideas, then you can sort out the good ones. __source__

We found $$T = c\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}},$$ where $$T$$ is the period of the pendulum, $$\ell$$ is the length of the pendulum, $$g$$ is Earth's gravitational acceleration, and $$c$$ is an unknown constant. We used that model to build two pendulums such that the ratio of their periods was $$2$$.

In this discussion problem, you will design your own experiment with the pendulum, write the methods in an initial post, and review two of your peers' methods.

Have you ever tried to follow someone's exact instructions and it didn't turn out the way you wanted? (https://youtu.be/FN2RM-CHkuI)

As you can see from the video, writing exact instructions can be challenging. Peer feedback is exceptionally helpful for improving the clarity of your writing. Here are a few tips: - Write simple, clear instructions with enough details for accurate replication. - Include which equipment you use. Example: "Use a meter stick to measure the length of your pencil." - Do not include extraneous steps like "measure twice, cut once", “collect all lab equipment” or “sharpen your pencil” or “meditate to clear your mind in preparation for accurate data collection”. - Using bullet points or numbered steps is perfectly acceptable.

For your experiment, you can choose to do this either in real life with a homemade pendulum, or you may use simulations like: (https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/pendulum-lab/latest/pendulum-lab_en.html)

**Instructions**

**$$1$$) Initial Post**

- Pick a (school appropriate) song. - Write out the name and artist. - Write out your methods to get the pendulum to swing to the beat of this song. Be specific enough that a peer could follow your exact instructions and get the same results. - Post methods and your song title/artist on the discussion board.

**$$2$$) Peer response**

- Read at least two other student posts on the discussion board and replicate their experiment using their exact methods. - Post your results. Were you able to get the pendulum to swing to the beat of the song? - Provide feedback for the methods you followed. Specifically note if any parts of the instructions were confusing.

**Peer Response Tips**

Reviewing another person's work is a valuable way to learn. Providing quality feedback is also a useful skill to master. Here are some tips to help you provide the most helpful, accurate, and consistent feedback possible: - Remember, English isn't everyone's native language. Focus primarily on how well you were able to follow their exact instructions. - When writing critical feedback, use a constructive and polite tone. - Don't forget to write what you liked about their post.

statement:
Scientists frequently have to learn new notation for concepts they already know in some other notation. In this problem, you will first learn a new notation for writing uncertainty, then practice with it.

---------------------

We've discussed writing uncertainties using the $$\pm$$ symbol. In this notation, $$x = 2.2 \pm 0.3 \;\mathrm{m},$$ means the absolute uncertainty in $$x$$ is $$0.3 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

Another way scientists report uncertainties is with a notation that looks like this:

$$G = 6.67430(15) \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}.$$

This is an equation for the __gravitational constant__, a number that's important to both Newton's and Einstein's theories of gravity.

The uncertainty in the last two digits of $$G$$ is represented by the parentheses. In other words, the gravitational constant is approximately $$G \approx 6.67430 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}},$$ but the last two digits might not be $$30.$$ They are uncertain by $$15,$$ so the last two digits could be anywhere from $$15$$ to $$45$$ and $$G$$ is probably in the range $$6.67415 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}} < G < 6.67445 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}$$

The same equation written in $$\pm$$ notation is $$G = \left(6.67430 \pm 0.00015 \right) \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}.$$

The absolute uncertainty in $$G$$ is $$\sigma_G = 0.00015 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-15} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}$$

----------------

Now we can do a practice problem with this new notation.

According to a group of scientists who worked on the space telescope __Planck__, the age of the universe is $$t_0 = 13.813(38) \times 10^9 \;\mathrm{year}.$$

What is the absolute uncertainty in the age of the universe, in years, according to these scientists?

statement:
Error (also called "uncertainty") can be __random__ or __systematic__.

Random error is error that's different every measurement you make. For example, when weighing items on a scale, you might place them randomly in slightly different positions on the tray, and this could affect the reading.

Systematic error affects every measurement you make in essentially the same way. For example, over time, the spring in a scale might get looser than it originally was. The scale compresses more than it should, resulting in all measurements being too large by about the same percentage. That would be systematic error.

Each of the following describes either random or systematic error. Choose the **one** that is random error.

**a)** In the cold weather, your ruler contracted a bit, and all your length measurements are now too long.

**b)** You can measure the volume of water with a __graduated cylinder__. The surface of the water will not be flat. Instead, it will climb slightly up the sides of the graduated cylinder by the same amount each measurement. To measure the volume, you are supposed to look at the lowest point in the center of the surface, called the __meniscus__, but instead you look at the highest point at the side each time. __image credit: Julie Mallon, https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~jmmallon/Inquiry1.pdf__

**c)** You are conducting an experiment in radioactivity and counting how many radioactive events occur using a device called a Geiger counter. Because radiation is an unpredictable process, sometimes your count is a little higher and sometimes a little lower.

**d)** Your scale has a "tare" button to make sure that zero mass reads out as zero, but you forget to use it. As a result, what the scale should read out as $$0 \;\mathrm{g}$$ it actually reads out as $$-3 \;\mathrm{g},$$ and all your mass measurements are too small by $$3 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

**e)** As you use an oscilloscope to measure electrical voltage, the oscilloscope heats up. This changes its electrical properties, and all your readings are off by a similar amount.

**f)** You're measuring the timing of some events using a video, but you have uncertainty about the frame rate (how many frames per second the video camera took). The camera's frame rate is perfectly steady, but you don't know exactly what that rate is.

statement:
Scientists can describe good measurements as both __accurate__ and __precise__, but these mean different things. (The noun forms are __accuracy__ and __precision__.) In this problem, you will review the difference between accuracy and precision, then decide whether various measurement procedures have high or low accuracy and high or low precision.

A measurement procedure has high precision when there is very little random error. This means that many repeated independent measurements will return very nearly the same every time. However, that result could still be wrong and be considered "precise". As long as all the results are very similar, the measurement is precise, regardless of how much systematic error there is.

A measurement has high accuracy when there is very little systematic error. This means that a large number of independent measurements is correct on average, with not overall bias to be too high or too low due to systematic error. However, a measurement can have high random error, causing lots of spread in the data, and still be considered accurate as long as the measurements are very close to the best possible value on average.

There are two competing definitions of accuracy. The one we will use in this class is that accuracy refers to how much systematic error there is and ignores random error, as we described above. However, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) defines "accuracy" as accounting for both random and systematic error. By their definition, a measurement process with high random error and low systematic error would not be accurate, but by our definition it would be.

Below are several histograms. Each summarizes the results from 1000 independent measurements made with the same measurement procedure. There are seven histograms, each representing a different measurement procedure.

All the measurement procedures are measuring the same dimensionless quantity. An eighth measuring procedure is known to be extremely accurate and extremely precise (but perhaps too expensive to use frequently) made the same measurement, coming up with a value of $$5.00.$$

For the purposes of this problem, we categorize precision as "high" if the standard deviation of the measurements is below .75 and "low" otherwise. We categorize accuracy as "high" if systematic error is below 1 and "low" otherwise. However, you should not need to perform any calculations; a rough understanding based on the shapes of the histograms should be sufficient.

statement:
In this problem, we'll practice the difference between __absolute error__, which we'll call $$\sigma,$$ and __relative error__, which we'll call $$\eta.$$ We'll also see some handy unit conversions that you might use later on. (But you don't need to memorize the unit conversions.)

----------

Many units are defined in terms of one another, and the conversion factors sometimes involve a large number of digits. For example, in class we saw that one pound mass in the Avoirdupois system is defined as $$ 1\;\mathrm{lb} = 0.45359237 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

Unlike a measurement reported with significant figures and uncertainty, this conversion is exact by definition.

Physical constants also sometimes have exact values as a byproduct of how units are defined. For example, the speed of light is exactly $$ c = 299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

The precise speed of light and pound-kilogram conversion factors may be difficult to remember because they have so many digits. Many people instead remember approximate values, such as $$2.2 \;\mathrm{lb} \approx 1 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ or $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Using these approximate values in a calculation will introduce some systematic error, but may be okay if the relative uncertainty in other parts of the calculation is already significantly larger than the relative error introduced by using an approximate unit conversion or physical constant.

Below is a table listing some exact physical constant and unit conversions. Below that are some approximate versions which are draggable. Order the approximate versions from greatest to least relative error.

In some cases, you may have to combine two exact conversions in order to evaluate how much relative error this is in one of the approximate conversions.

Remember that the relative error in a quantity is the absolute error divided by the quantity itself. For example, the absolute error in the speed of light approximation is $$\sigma = 300{,}000{,}000 \;\mathrm{m/s} - 299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s} = 207{,}542 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$

This may seem like a lot of error because $$207{,}542 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ is a fast speed, but the relative error is $$\eta = \dfrac{207{,}542 \;\mathrm{m/s}}{299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s}} \approx 0.00069,$$ so the relative error is quite small, and $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ is a good approximation despite the large-seeming absolute error.

$$\begin{aligned} {} & \text{\large Conversion or Constant} & \text{\large \,\,\,Exact } & \text{\large \,Equation} \\ \hline {} & \text{pounds to kilograms} \quad\quad\quad & 1 \;\mathrm{lb} & = 0.45359237 \;\mathrm{kg} \\ {} & \text{miles to inches} & 1 \;\mathrm{mile} &= 63{,}360 \;\mathrm{in} \\ {} & \text{inches to centimeters} & 1 \;\mathrm{in} &= 2.54 \;\mathrm{cm} \\ {} & \text{calories to joules} & 1 \;\mathrm{cal} &= 4.184 \;\mathrm{J} \\ {} & \text{speed of light} & c &= 299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s} \\ {} & \text{Planck's constant} & h & = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34} \;\mathrm{J \cdot s}\\ {} & \text{elementary charge} & e & = 1.602176634 \times 10^{-19} \;\mathrm{C}\\ \end{aligned}$$

In 1913, Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed what became known as the __Bohr model__ of the atom.

In the Bohr model, an important quantity is the amount of energy needed to completely pull an electron off of a hydrogen atom. This amount of energy is called the __Rydberg,__ $$\mathrm{Ry}.$$ Bohr found this formula for it:

$$ 1 \;\mathrm{Ry} = \dfrac{m_e e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2}.$$

Although you can solve this problem without them, the meanings of the variables are: $$\begin{aligned} m_e: & \text{ mass of an electron} \\ e: & \text{ electric charge of a proton}\\ \epsilon_0: & \text{ permittivity of the vacuum, a physical constant related to electromagnetism}\\ h: & \text{ Planck's constant, a physical constant related to quantum mechanics} \end{aligned}$$ You don't need to know the values of the constants in this problem in order to solve the problem.

Bohr also simplified his formula by introducing the __fine structure constant__ $$\alpha,$$ $$ \alpha = \dfrac{e^2}{2 \epsilon_0 h}.$$

desc: The goal of this problem is to explore the relationship between how units are defined and the values of constants. For example, the speed of light is approximately $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Imagine we doubled how long the meter is. That wouldn't change how long…
statement:
The goal of this problem is to explore the relationship between how units are defined and the values of constants. For example, the speed of light is approximately $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Imagine we doubled how long the meter is. That wouldn't change how long it takes light to get from place to place. For example, if we shine light from one mountaintop to the next and it used to take $$10^{-4}$$ seconds to go from mountaintop to mountaintop, it still would take $$10^{-4}$$ seconds after the meter redefinition.

However, if we doubled the length of the meter, we'd cut the number of meters between the mountaintops in half. If it used to be about $$3\times 10^5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ between mountaintops, with the new, longer meter, we'd only need $$1.5 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ to span the same distance. That means light would now travel only $$1.5 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$10^{-4} \;\mathrm{s},$$ so the speed of light would be $$c \approx 1.5 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ after we doubled the length of a meter. Light would still go just as fast, but with the new unit system we'd refer to that speed with a different number.

Notice that $$\mathrm{m}$$ appears in the numerator of $$\mathrm{m/s},$$ and when we double the length of a meter, we cut the speed of light in half. If we were to double the how long a second is, that would give light twice as much time to travel in what we call "one second", and the speed of light would double. $$\mathrm{s}$$ are in the denominator of $$\mathrm{m/s},$$ and doubling the duration of a second doubles the speed of light.

Your job in this problem is to extend this reasoning to the gravitational constant. As you think about this problem, remember that in the gravitational constant, the dimensions are not all to the first power or negative first power, like they are in the speed of light.

----------

We saw in the prereading that Newton's gravitational constant is $$G \approx 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \dfrac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{s}^2}.$$

Suppose we want to redefine some units to change the numerical part of Newton's gravitational constant so that instead of $$6.67 \times 10^{-11},$$ it becomes $$10^{-10},$$ which is a bit larger. That is, we want to make a unit redefinition so that $$G_{\rm after \; redefinition} = 1\times 10^{-10} \dfrac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{s}^2} $$

In this equation, at least one of the meter, second, or kilogram would have to change to a new value.

For example, if we doubled the mass of the kilogram to define a new kilogram, $$G$$ would also double. This would not solve the problem, because then $$G \approx 1.3348 \times 10^{-10} \dfrac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{s}^2},$$ but instead of doubling the kilogram, we could multiply it by some number a bit less than two such that the numerical part of $$G$$ came out exactly to $$10^{-10}.$$

Find the number we would need to multiply the kilogram by to change $$G$$ in this way. Then find the number we would need to multiply the second by to change $$G$$ in the same way, assuming we don't change the kilogram and only change the second. A ball of mass $$m$$ moving at velocity $$v$$ approaches a ball of mass $$M$$ that is sitting stationary.

$$v$$ is positive for motion to the right and negative for motion to the left.

Here's a picture of the situation:

We have drawn the ball of mass $$m$$ smaller than the ball of mass $$M,$$ but we imagine that either ball could be the more massive one, depending on the values of $$m$$ and $$M.$$

The balls collide and bounce off each other. The ball on the right winds up moving to the right at a velocity $$v_M$$ and the ball on the left will, in this example, bounce off to the left, moving with some velocity $$v_m.$$

Over the rest of this problem (which has several parts), we'll find a formula for $$v_m.$$

statement:
Recall that, in the prereading, we learned about several different models for DNA. These are summarized in the image below:

__Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.__

Each model is applicable to solving different scientific problems. **Connect each problem to the single most relevant model.**

The connections are one-to-one.

**Scientific Problems:**

**(A)** If a strand of DNA sits on its own in water, it will uncoil. It doesn't become straight. Instead, the random motion of the molecules in the water leads the DNA to have a winding, random shape. How does the shape change as we change the temperature of the water?

__Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.__

**(B)** __RNA polymerase__ is a complicated protein that binds to the DNA and copies a piece of its genetic material. Where will RNA polymerase latch on to the DNA molecule?

**(C)** Cells need to control which genes they are using at any given time. In one example, part of the cell's procedure to control its genes involves bending a short segment of DNA into a loop to bring two parts that are usually separated right next to each other. How much energy does it takes to curve the DNA segment into a circle and form this loop?

**(D)** __Cystic fibrosis__ is a genetic disorder that can cause poor lung function. Where are the genes related to cystic fibrosis located in the human genome? Can we detect cystic fibrosis in a human embryo?

**(E)** When the fluid near DNA is salty, ions (atoms with electric charge) in the water are attracted or repelled from the DNA because of the electric charge on the DNA molecule. How do the charge on DNA and saltiness of the environment affect genetic processes?

**Models**

**sequence model** The sequence model ignores the physical structure of DNA and only reports the human genome as a list of nucleotides. Groups of nucleotides form genes. This model is useful for understanding DNA as genetic information. For example, it could tell us which gene tells the body how to make a certain protein, or which gene is copied incorrectly in a certain genetic disease.

**binding site model** Cells have many complicated proteins in them called __molecular machines__. Some molecular machines attach themselves to the DNA, unwind the DNA, and make copies of it. The binding site model is useful for studying this process of molecular machines attaching to the DNA.

**charged rod model** DNA has negative __electric charge__ because it has more electrons (which have negative charge) than protons (which have positive charge). In the charged rod model, we study how the charge on the DNA interacts with any charged particles in the nearby environment. This model is __not__ concerned with bending of the rod, despite the drawing showing some bending.

**elastic rod model** The elastic rod model views DNA as a series of springs that must be stretched or compressed when the shape of the DNA changes. It is useful for thinking about forces or energy in curved pieces of DNA, especially for short DNA strands.

**random walk model** The random walk model thinks of longer segments of DNA (about 50 base pairs each) as straight lines, but each straight line goes off in a random direction. This model is useful for studying the behavior of DNA (and many other processes) in a random environment, like when it's immersed in a fluid and molecules strike it randomly from all directions.

statement:
In physics classes, it's common to model __projectiles__ - any object that is thrown or hurled in some way. Below are some different types of projectiles and some physical effects that affect projectiles. **Connect each projectile to the effects critically important for understanding its motion.**

By "critically important", we mean any model that leaves out the effect would be very unlikely to be useful for any meaningful prediction, even for an order of magnitude estimate.

There are no limits on how many connections you are allowed to make.

**Projectiles**

**comet**: Comets are icy objects orbiting the sun. They usually have very elliptical orbits, meaning they're much closer to the sun at some times than at others. They orbit in deep outer space, where there is no atmosphere.

**paper airplane**: Imagine a student tossing a small, hand-folded paper airplane and hoping to make it fly across a classroom, much further than a rock would go if tossed with the same initial speed.

**long jumper**: A long jumper is an athlete in track and field. Top long jumpers travel about $$8 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in the air, so the total mass of air they interact with is much less than their own mass.

**dust speck**: A small speck of dust, when released into the air, is so light that moves along with the air next to it. If it has some initial motion relative to the air around it, that motion will be damped out before the speck moves more than a minuscule distance. Small air currents can carry a dust speck around for a long time.

**Effects**

$$v_0$$: This is the effect of changing the initial speed of the projectile. In most cases, the faster the initial speed, the further the projectile will go. This effect is important for any sort of projectile motion where if the initial speed is different, the projectile would take a significantly different path.

**Air effects**: a projectile can interact with the air in several ways. The projectile will hit the air, and the air will put a force on the projectile called "air drag". Depending on the shape of the object, the air can also exert an upward force called "lift". These forces are usually only important when the total mass of the air that the projectiles interacts with is at least comparable to the mass of the projectile itself. In other words, heavy things thrown a short distance don't need to worry about the effects of air, but light things do. Heavy things thrown a very long distance will also need to account for air effects, since they move through so much air that the air they move through has as much or more mass than the projectile itself.

**Non-uniform Gravity**: Although we usually model gravity as a uniform force for projectiles, it isn't. The further from the Earth (or sun) a projectile is, the weaker the gravitational pull on it. This effect becomes important when the distance of the projectile from the center of the Earth (or sun) changes by a large fraction during its flight. For this effect, you are not choosing whether or not gravity is an important influence on the projectile. Instead, you're imagining a default model where gravity is uniform - the same over the entire path the projectile follow. Then you're deciding whether the correction of __non-uniform__ gravity is a vital correction for modeling the projectile.

Part A. For this problem, you will need a little background information on __protein translation__, the process by which living cells create proteins.

**Background on protein translation**

When cells need to build new proteins, they do this using __RNA__ and __ribosomes__. The RNA molecules are copies of bits of DNA in the cell. They look like long strings. A ribosome is a molecule machine that latches onto an RNA on one side and moves steadily down the RNA. As the ribosome moves, it reads the sequence of the RNA and uses it to determine what protein to build from raw materials in the cell. This process is called __protein translation__.

Many ribosomes can latch onto an RNA molecule at the same time, and they all move down the RNA building new proteins. One ribosome cannot pass by another ribosome from behind. Instead a faster-moving ribosome will have to wait behind the ribosome in front of it. In this way, ribosomes on an RNA have some similarity to cars in traffic. If too many ribosome latch onto the same RNA molecule, there will be crowding that slows things down.

Scientists want to know how quickly new proteins can be made with this system. We will examine a simple model for ribosomes moving down an RNA molecule to study the rate at which proteins are made.

**TASEP** One model used to study protein translation is TASEP, which stands for __Totally Asymmetric Stochastic Exclusion Process__. "Totally asymmetric" means that the objects in the model can only move in one direction. "Stochastic" means that there is some randomness in the model. "Exclusion" means that the objects cannot pass through or by each other.

You can use an implementation of the TASEP model at this link (Open this in a new tab.)

You will see a line of gray squares represent an RNA molecule. You'll also see black dots moving through the gray squares from left to right. These represent ribosomes moving down the RNA. When a ribosome gets to the end of the RNA molecule, it can disappear from the model, representing finishing its protein and detaching from the RNA. New ribosomes appear at the beginning of the RNA molecule.

The simulation counts how many proteins are completed per unit time. This is called the flux. The long term average flux is equal to the number of ribosomes that have left the end of the mRNA molecule divided by number of timesteps the simulation has run.

**Thin air and running speed**

**Tailwind** During Beamon's jump, there was a wind pushing at his back.

Part B. To continue our estimate surrounding Bob Beamon's long jump, we'll need a model for the long jump. Eventually, we will find the total distance the long jumper jumps, and this is the first step. In this part of the problem, we'll introduce a model. Your job is to think about the vertical motion of the long jumper in the model.

----------------

A simple model for the long jump is that first, an athlete runs as fast as they can down the runway, attaining a top speed of $$v_r.$$ This stage is called the "run up".

Next, at the end of the runway, the athlete leaps into the air. This stage is called the "takeoff". During the takeoff, the athlete's goal is to jump up as high as possible. They have already attained their top horizontal speed and can't run any faster, so they don't think about adding horizontal speed during the takeoff. Instead, they maintain the same horizontal speed while adding as much vertical speed as they can. We will assume that during takeoff, the athlete jumps upward with a speed $$v_j.$$

In this model, when the athlete jumps into the air, they are moving diagonally upward and forward. They still have a forward speed $$v_r$$ from their run, and they have an upward speed $$v_j$$ from their jump.

During the jump, we can analyze the athlete's horizontal and vertical motions separately. While in the air, the athlete moves forward with constant speed $$v_r.$$ In the vertical direction, the athlete begins with upward speed $$v_j,$$ but gravity pulls downward on the athlete, reducing their vertical speed down to zero at the height of the jump, and then down to $$-v_j$$ when the athlete hits the ground.

To find the total distance of the jump, we can consider how fast the athlete moved forward and how long they were in the air.

statement:
Part A. We've already studied the question: "What is the terminal velocity of an object falling through air?"

If we wanted to measure terminal velocity, we could see how far something falls, measure how long that takes, and divide to get the terminal velocity.

On the other hand, that method would fail if the object were still accelerating up to its terminal velocity when we took the measurement. To measure terminal velocity, we want to drop something, let it fall until it reaches its terminal velocity (or gets very close to it), and only then begin measuring distance and time for the rest of the fall.

To help with this, in this problem we'll address a different question:

"How far does an object have to fall through the air before it reaches its terminal velocity?"

We know that when we let something go, gravity pulls it to the ground. The speed of the object gets faster and faster as it falls. The rate that the speed increases is the object's __acceleration__. As we've seen, the acceleration of objects dropped near the surface of Earth (ignoring any wind drag) is $$g \approx 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Assuming there is no air drag, the speed is $$|v| = gt,$$ where $$t$$ is the time the object has been falling.

We've already estimated the terminal velocity to be $$|v_{\rm terminal}| \approx \sqrt{\dfrac{2 mg}{\rho A}}.$$

(We have left $$C_D$$ out of this equation because we estimated that it was close to $$1,$$ and so doesn't have much effect.)

As a simple model, assume that an object that has dropped follows the equation $$|v| = gt$$ until it reaches terminal velocity. This is not completely accurate, but okay for our estimation. Combine $$|v| = gt$$ and $$v_{\rm terminal} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 mg}{\rho A}}$$ to estimate the time it takes a falling object to reach terminal velocity.

Next, multiply the terminal velocity by the time you just found. This gives an estimate for the distance $$d$$ something needs to fall before reaching a speed close to its terminal velocity. You should get an equation for $$d$$ in terms of $$m, \rho, A, C_D,$$ and $$g.$$

Find this equation, then use it to estimate how far a piece of notebook paper needs to fall through air before approximately reaching its terminal velocity.

There will still be some slow-moving molecules in a hot gas and some fast-moving molecules in a cold gas, but taken as a whole, faster speeds means hotter.

The __second law of thermodynamics__ says that heat always moves from hotter places to colder places as long as there is no energy being used to transfer the heat.

For example, suppose we have a box with a wall in the middle. There is some warm gas on the left of the wall and cool gas on the right. Then according to the second law of thermodynamics, heat can only move from left to right unless there is outside energy used to move it the opposite way. Not even a little heat is allowed to go the opposite direction.

In 1867, Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell invented a thought experiment that cast doubt on the second law of thermodynamics.

In this thought experiment, there is a box with warm gas on one side (side B) and cool gas on the other side (side A). There is a barrier in the middle of the box keeping the gasses separate. The box and barrier don't allow any heat to pass through them. The laws of physics say that in this situation, the two sides' temperatures would not change over time.

Next, Maxwell imagined a creature that could see gas molecules. Maxwell imagined the creature installing a trap door in the wall between the warm and cool gas. The creature could open or close the door whenever it wants without spending any energy because the door had zero friction.

The creature watched the air molecules on side A, the cool side. It waited until, by chance, a particularly fast-moving air molecule from the cool gas was approaching the trap door. The creature opened the door to let only that air molecule pass, then closed the door again.

Then the creature watched the gas on the side B, the warm side. It waited until a particularly slow-moving air molecule from the warm gas was about to hit the trap door. It again opened the door and let the molecule through to the cool side.

Maxwell imagined the creature repeating this over and over. Eventually, a lot of fast-moving molecules would have moved from the cold air to the warm air, and a lot of slow-moving molecules would haved moved from the warm air to the cool air. This would raise the average speed of molecules in the warm air and lower the average speed of molecules in the cold air. As a result, the warm air would get warmer and the cold air would get colder, even though the creature hadn't used up any energy.

If such a creature could exist within the laws of physics, it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

Scientists were confused by this thought experiment for a long time. They still believed that the second law of thermodynamics was correct, but the thought experiment seemed to show it was not correct. Many people proposed resolutions to the paradox of Maxwell's thought experiment.

Which one of the following, if it were correct, would be a valid resolution to the puzzle of Maxwell's thought experiment?

No such creature has evolved on Earth.

Scientists tried to build a version of Maxwell's thought experiment, but it was too hard to measure the speeds of the molecules with current technology.

According to the law of quantum mechanics, if the creature did exist, the act of measuring the speeds of the molecules would have to use energy, and that energy would be enough to move the heat from cool to warm air via conventional means (like using electricity to remove heat from an already-cool refrigerator)

Although the creature could move heat from cool to warm air without using energy, it could only do it for a little while. Eventually it would run out of molecules to trade back and forth and have to stop.

Real doors usually have a little bit of friction in them, so the creature's door isn't realistic.

Imagine two boxes, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ of equal mass. At time $$t_1$$ the boxes are held stationary with a compressed spring between them. The spring stores some potential energy, which we call $$S.$$

The boxes are released and the spring pushes them apart so that all the potential energy in the spring is converted to kinetic energy in the boxes. At this point, the boxes move in opposite directions, each at speed $$v.$$ We can call this time $$t_2.$$

Once the spring has been released, it can be ignored. It has no mass.
